title: Memento Pattern
oneLiner: Captures an object's internal state so it can be restored later, without exposing that state to the outside world.

hero.name: The Historian
hero.catchphrase: I remember exactly who you were. Just ask, and I'll bring it back.
hero.power: Snapshots an object's private internal state and can restore it later, without ever exposing that state publicly.
hero.weakness: Every snapshot costs memory — keep an unlimited undo history and The Historian will quietly eat all your RAM.
hero.origin: The Historian appeared after a text editor's undo feature was implemented by making every private field public, just so the undo code outside the class could read and restore them.

story.problem: To implement undo, a text editor's `content` and `cursorPosition` fields were made public just so external undo code could read and restore them — breaking encapsulation for every other caller too.
story.solution: The Historian lets the editor create a private, opaque `Memento` snapshot of its own state. The undo manager stores mementos but can't read or modify their contents — only the editor that created one can restore from it.
story.result: Undo works perfectly, and the editor's internal fields go back to being genuinely private. Nothing outside the editor can peek at or tamper with a snapshot.

before: Internal fields made public just to support undo
Any code can read or corrupt editor internals
Undo logic is entangled with the editor's implementation
after: Snapshots are opaque — only the editor can read its own memento
Undo logic only touches an opaque history of snapshots

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: The Editor class has every field marked public, with a comment: '// public for undo, sorry'.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Now anything in the codebase can directly mutate the editor's cursor position. We broke encapsulation just to support undo.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Historian appears holding a sealed, labeled envelope — a snapshot nobody but the editor can open.
panels.speaker: The Historian
panels.dialogue: You don't need to expose your fields. Let me hold a snapshot instead — sealed, private, restorable only by you.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Editor.save() returns an opaque Memento. Editor.restore(memento) reads it back — nobody else can.
panels.speaker: The Historian
panels.dialogue: The undo manager just stores my sealed envelopes in order. It never opens them. Only you can.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Every editor field goes back to private. Undo still works flawlessly.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Encapsulation restored, undo still works perfectly. The undo manager has no idea what's actually inside a memento.

useWhen: You need undo/rollback functionality that captures an object's internal state at a point in time.
You want to snapshot state without breaking encapsulation by exposing private fields.
You need to restore an object to a known-good state after a failed operation.
avoidWhen: The object's state is trivial (one or two primitive fields) — a plain copy is simpler than a formal Memento.
You need unlimited history depth with large objects — memory cost can become a real problem.
The 'state' includes external resources (open connections, file handles) that can't be meaningfully snapshotted and restored.
commonMistakes: Making memento fields public 'just this once', undoing the entire point of the pattern.
Keeping an unbounded undo history for large objects, silently consuming huge amounts of memory over a long session.
Snapshotting mutable objects by reference instead of by value, so 'restoring' a memento doesn't actually revert anything.
Confusing Memento (snapshot + restore an object's own state) with Command's undo (reverses an action's side effects) — they're often combined, but solve different problems.
explanation.realWorldExample: Undo/redo history in editors, database transaction rollback/savepoints, and game save states (a snapshot of the entire game world you can reload) are all Memento in practice.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How is this different from just deep-cloning the object?

conversation.speaker: The Historian
conversation.message: A clone is a full, usable copy — anyone can read and use it. A memento is deliberately opaque. Whoever HOLDS it (like an undo manager) can't peek inside; only the original object can read its own snapshot back.

conversation.speaker: The Historian
conversation.message: Memory. Every snapshot is a real copy of state. Keep infinite undo history for large objects, and I'll happily eat all your RAM without complaint.

codeBattle.scenario: Your game needs a 'save point' system that captures the entire world state and can restore it exactly later, without exposing the game engine's internal data structures to the save/load UI code.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Historian lets the game engine create opaque save-state snapshots that the save/load UI can store and pass back, without ever reading or tampering with the engine's internals.

quiz.question: What does Memento capture, and who can read it?
options: An object's internal state, readable only by the object that created it
An object's public methods, readable by anyone
A log of every method call ever made
A copy of the entire application's memory
quiz.answer: An object's internal state, readable only by the object that created it
quiz.explanation: Opacity to outside code is exactly what preserves encapsulation while still enabling snapshot/restore.

quiz.question: What problem does Memento solve that a plain public state copy doesn't?
options: It preserves encapsulation — the snapshot is opaque to everything except the originating object
It removes the need for the object to have any state at all
It guarantees only one snapshot can ever exist
quiz.answer: It preserves encapsulation — the snapshot is opaque to everything except the originating object
quiz.explanation: A public copy exposes internals to any caller; a proper memento keeps that state private outside the originator.

quiz.question: What's the main cost/risk of using Memento?
options: Each snapshot consumes memory, and unbounded history can grow very large
It requires the object to have exactly one field
It can only be used with immutable objects
quiz.answer: Each snapshot consumes memory, and unbounded history can grow very large
quiz.explanation: Snapshots are real copies of state — keeping too many of them, especially for large objects, adds up fast.

quiz.question: How does Memento relate to Command's undo functionality?
options: They're often combined — Command triggers the action, Memento captures state to restore if it needs to be reversed
They are the exact same pattern
Memento can only be used without Command
Command replaces the need for Memento entirely
quiz.answer: They're often combined — Command triggers the action, Memento captures state to restore if it needs to be reversed
quiz.explanation: Many undo systems use Command to represent the action and Memento to represent the state to roll back to.
